title: Japan household spending falls for ninth straight month, but drop smaller than expected
body: The mixed readings are unlikely to shift Bank of Japan rate expectations decisively in either direction, limiting the immediate impact on the yen and Japanese government bonds. A smaller annual decline offers modest support to the case for tightening, but the weak monthly gain and nine straight contractions undercut the argument that consumption is recovering alongside wages. That gap between rising real wages and falling spending is the key tension for policymakers, and further evidence that households are saving rather than spending would argue for patience. For Japanese retailers and consumer stocks, the data point to a slow and uneven recovery in domestic demand. --- Japanese workers have had eight straight months of real pay rises, but their wallets have stayed shut for nine, and that is the puzzle the Bank of Japan has to solve.

title: Weekend oil trading during this Iran war is crypto's turning point, says Citrini
body: Citrini's record of moving markets gives the report weight, and the immediate spike in some named tokens shows how sensitive thinly traded crypto assets are to high-profile research. Listed names it flagged, including Coinbase, Robinhood and Circle, could see attention when US trading resumes, though one report is unlikely to shift their fundamentals. For oil, the most relevant thread is weekend trading: with Iran strike options reported ready and Gulf tanker attacks elevated, blockchain-based venues such as Hyperliquid may again set the first price for crude if events move while traditional futures markets are closed. That would test the argument in real time. --- Citrini's argument is simple: AI agents never sleep, so the money they move will need markets that never close, and crypto has spent fifteen years building just that.

title: Is AI giving the US economy a case of Dutch disease? From Dutch gas to American chips.
body: If the argument holds, the AI build-out is a source of upward pressure on bond yields, power prices and wages for scarce technical staff, which would keep financing costs high for sectors outside technology. That fits with this week's 24-year high in 10-year Treasury yields, which Bloomberg partly attributed to AI-related corporate borrowing. For equities, the thesis implies widening divergence between AI beneficiaries and consumer-facing companies facing squeezed household budgets, a pattern visible in PepsiCo's North American results. Energy markets are a complicating factor, as Iran-war oil prices are lifting electricity and input costs independently of AI demand. - The Netherlands found gas and watched the rest of its economy wilt; Derek Thompson's worry is that America has found AI and is running the same experiment.

title: PepsiCo lowers profit guidance as cost pressure and a cautious US consumer bite
body: The muted share reaction, a modest intraday gain largely given back by the close, suggests investors weighed the quarterly beat against a clear downgrade to profit expectations. Stripping out the one-off tariff refund leaves underlying margins under more pressure than the headline numbers imply, which may keep analysts cautious on earnings estimates. With energy-linked input costs elevated as the Iran war keeps oil prices high, and a cautious US consumer forcing price cuts on snacks, the results are an early warning sign for consumer staples ahead of peers' earnings. Planned structural cost cuts give management a lever, but the details and timing are not yet known. --- Posting this ICYMI. --- PepsiCo cleared the bar for the quarter, but strip out a tariff refund and cut guidance, and the picture is a company selling more abroad while working harder for every dollar at home.

title: How a (negative!) $20 billion gap opened up in OpenAI's revenue figures
body: The gap underlines how difficult it is to compare private AI developers, whose headline numbers shape valuations in some of the largest private funding rounds on record. For investors in listed AI exposure, from cloud providers to chipmakers, the episode is a reminder that annualised revenue figures from private labs are not audited results and can vary by accounting choice rather than underlying demand. Accounting method will come under closer scrutiny if either company moves toward a public listing, where reported revenue and standard earnings disclosures replace investor-facing metrics. Profit claims excluding stock-based compensation, and made before large computing commitments take effect, are likely to face the same scepticism. --- Posting this ICYMI. Its negative for equites, at the amrgin. --- OpenAI's $70 billion revenue figure turns out to be $50 billion counted its own way, a $20 billion lesson in why AI companies' headline numbers rarely compare like-for-like.

title: Capitalist conditions have weakened worldwide since 2009, University of Virginia index shows
body: The index is not a market mover, but it supports the case that wealth flows toward jurisdictions with strong property rights and open capital markets, which favours established hubs such as Switzerland, Singapore and Hong Kong. The finding that capital markets and banking are the weakest pillars globally points to underdeveloped financial systems as a persistent constraint on investment in many economies. Western Europe's decline, alongside the exit of the UK, Ireland, Finland and the Netherlands from the top ten, adds to the narrative of a region losing competitiveness for mobile capital. Investors may read the widening regional divergence as reinforcing a preference for Central Asian and selected emerging markets over parts of Latin America. --- The world's most capitalist economies look a lot like its favourite places to park private wealth, while the system as a whole has been quietly losing ground for 16 years.

title: Morgan Stanley bond manager turns bullish on Treasuries for first time in a decade
body: A top-performing manager adding duration near the highs is a notable contrarian signal for Treasuries, though he still allows for yields to overshoot by another 10 to 15 basis points before peaking. His case rests on the Fed's hiking path slowing growth, so any sign that energy-driven inflation forces the central bank to go further would test it. For oil, the link runs both ways: Iran-war energy prices helped drive the bond selloff, and a renewed crude spike would add to inflation pressure and delay any rally in yields. Widening spreads for weaker corporate and sovereign borrowers suggest tighter financial conditions are starting to bite. --- After a decade on the sidelines, one of Wall Street's best-performing bond managers says yields near 5.4% now pay investors enough to bet that the Fed will break growth before it breaks the bond market.

title: Japan Personal Spending Falls the Least in 3 Months
body: Japan's household spending declined 3.1% year-on-year in August 2026, a smaller drop than in July and better than market expectations of a 3.6% fall. Despite this improvement, it was the ninth consecutive month of contraction, reflecting continued consumer caution amid persistent inflation. Even so, the decline was the mildest since May. By category, spending remained weak across most segments. Expenditure on food fell 1.4% (vs -1.3% in July), utilities dropped 5.2% (vs -9.2%), healthcare was down 1.9% (vs -6.0%), clothing plunged 8.7% (vs -0.3%), housing decreased 5.8% (vs -16.4%), and education spending contracted 12.3% (vs -5.4%). Outlays on furniture and household goods slipped 6.3%, reversing a 0.7% increase in July, while spending on culture and recreation fell 4.3%, compared with 4.8% growth previously. In contrast, transport and communication spending returned to growth, rising 0.2% after an 8.5% decline in July. On a seasonally adjusted month-on-month basis, overall household expenditure inched up 0.1%, marking a second consecutive monthly gain but slowing sharply from July and undershooting forecasts of a 0.5% increase. title: Japan's Household Spending Nearly Stalls in August, Slipping to 0.1% MoM
body: Japan's household spending growth slowed sharply in August 2026, signaling weakening consumer momentum in the world's third-largest economy. Month-over-month, household expenditures rose just 0.1%, down from a 0.5% increase in July 2026, according to data updated on 8 October 2026. The month-over-month measure compares the change in spending each month with the previous one, and August's reading suggests that the modest improvement seen in July did not carry forward with the same strength. While spending remained marginally positive, the near-flat gain points to more cautious consumption by Japanese households, a key pillar of domestic demand. For policymakers and markets, the deceleration raises questions about the durability of Japan's consumption recovery, as even slight pullbacks in household outlays can reverberate through broader economic activity. Investors will be watching upcoming data closely for signs of whether August's softness is a temporary pause or the start of a more entrenched slowdown in consumer spending. body: Crude oil retreated toward $91 per barrel on Friday, paring gains from the previous session after President Donald Trump wrote on social media that the US was engaged in "productive discussions" with Iran and would avoid attacking the country before the midterm elections. Trump also asserted that record volumes of crude were moving through the Strait of Hormuz, while emphasizing that the US naval blockade of Iranian ports would remain fully in force. Subsequent reports, however, indicated that the US had drawn up plans for three days of strikes on Iran, focusing on drone and missile stockpiles, energy infrastructure and other strategic targets. At the same time, Hurricane Isaias threatened offshore production in the Gulf of Mexico, leading producers to shut in roughly 1.3 million barrels per day of crude output. title: NZX 50 Poised for 2nd Straight Weekly Decline
body: The NZX 50 fell 51 points, or 0.4%, to 13,641 in Friday morning trading, hitting its lowest level since September 16 and reversing a modest gain from the previous session. The benchmark followed Wall Street lower, as renewed selling in technology stocks and a further rise in oil prices weighed on global sentiment. Persistent strength in oil prices continued to stoke concerns about inflation and the prospect of further interest rate hikes. Caution also prevailed ahead of next week's releases of New Zealand food inflation and business PMI data, as well as inflation figures from the US and China that could offer additional insight into economic conditions in both economies. Losses were broad-based, with financials, industrials, and consumer discretionary names exerting the most downward pressure on the index. Notable decliners included Infratil (-2.2%), Ventia Services Group (-1.6%), South Port NZ (-1.2%), and Auckland International Airport (-1.1%). title: Uruguay Central Bank Hikes Policy Rate
body: Uruguay's central bank has raised its monetary policy rate by 25 basis points to 6.0%, with the aim of keeping inflation expectations anchored and guiding inflation toward its 4.5% target over the two-year monetary policy horizon. The bank noted that ongoing international geopolitical tensions continue to drive up energy prices and, indirectly, the prices of other tradable goods, leading to upward revisions in inflation expectations. In this context, policy rates at major central banks, as well as yields in international financial markets, have also moved higher. Domestically, the Uruguayan economy is showing signs of resilience after sector-specific and weather-related shocks temporarily dampened activity. The bank stated that inflation remains on a convergent path toward the target as these temporary effects dissipate, but cautioned that persistent geopolitical and climate-related shocks continue to pose significant risks to prices and inflation expectations. title: Ibovespa Gains Ahead of Election Runoff Poll
body: The Ibovespa advanced 0.9% on Thursday to close at 206,220, as investors awaited the first Datafolha poll for the presidential runoff, scheduled for release shortly after the market close. In Sunday's first-round election, Bolsonaro finished ahead of Lula, defying most pre-election polls and driving the index to a record high on Monday, led by financial stocks. Market participants view the senator as more fiscally conservative, a stance that resonates in an environment of high domestic interest rates and sluggish economic activity. His economic team is reportedly weighing spending cuts equivalent to around 2% of GDP. Among major movers, financial stocks were mixed: B3 rose 2%, while Bradesco slipped 1.3%. Petrobras gained 2.1%, tracking the sharp increase in international oil prices. Retail names also underpinned the index, with Magazine Luiza surging 5.6%. In contrast, Vale extended its losing streak to a fourth consecutive session, dropping 1.6% as iron ore prices in China fell to an 18-month low. title: Fed Reserve Balances Edge Higher to $3.022 Trillion, Signaling Continued Liquidity Support
body: Reserve balances with Federal Reserve Banks in the United States have risen to $3.022 trillion, up from the previous level of $2.881 trillion, according to data updated on 8 October 2026. The increase in reserve balances suggests that liquidity conditions in the U.S. banking system remain ample, with commercial banks holding more funds on deposit at the Federal Reserve. While the data alone does not indicate policy direction, a higher reserve level can reflect ongoing support from the Fed's balance sheet operations or changes in banks' demand for safe, highly liquid assets. Market participants will be watching subsequent releases to determine whether this uptick marks the beginning of a sustained build‑up in reserves or a temporary fluctuation tied to short‑term funding dynamics and technical factors in money markets. title: Fed Balance Sheet Edges Higher to $6.748 Trillion, Signaling Ongoing Cautious Stance
body: The U.S. Federal Reserve's balance sheet has inched up to $6.748 trillion, from a previous level of $6.743 trillion, according to data updated on 8 October 2026. The latest figures point to a modest expansion of $5 billion in the central bank's total assets. While the move is incremental, any change in the Fed's balance sheet is closely watched by investors as a barometer of liquidity conditions and the central bank's broader policy stance. The uptick suggests that, despite the push in recent years to pare back pandemic-era stimulus, the Fed remains active in managing its portfolio and providing targeted support where needed. Market participants will now be assessing whether this slight increase reflects temporary technical factors or the early stages of a more sustained shift in the Fed's approach to balance sheet management, with implications for bond markets, funding costs, and overall financial conditions in the United States. title: Crude Oil Gains on Renewed Supply Disruptions
body: Crude oil prices climbed toward $91 a barrel in a turbulent session on Thursday, driven by escalating Iranian attacks on tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz and mounting concerns that Hurricane Isaias could disrupt US offshore production in the Gulf of Mexico. Over the past week, nine tankers have been attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz, threatening the fragile recovery in crude flows through this critical chokepoint. About 9.5 million barrels per day left the strait in the week ended Tuesday, roughly 30% below normal pre-war levels. In the Gulf of Mexico, oil companies have shut in around 500,000 barrels per day—about 25% of offshore output—as Hurricane Isaias tracks toward the coasts of Alabama, Mississippi, and the Florida Panhandle. Prices had earlier pulled back from session highs after US President Donald Trump stated that Washington would not launch attacks on Iran before the November midterm elections. That followed earlier reports suggesting Trump and his national security team had been weighing renewed strikes in the coming weeks. title: US Stocks Retreat on Tech Selloff
body: US stock indices finished broadly lower on Thursday after the Financial Times reported that OpenAI's revenue was significantly below levels previously cited by other media. The S&P 500 declined 0.5%, and the Nasdaq fell 1.4%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average bucked the trend to close 52 points higher. According to documents reviewed by the FT, OpenAI's annualized revenue is about $50 billion, compared with earlier estimates of roughly $70 billion. The revision rekindled worries about the profitability of large language model developers and the durability of massive AI infrastructure spending—key drivers of both this year's equity rally and US GDP growth. Chipmakers led the pullback, with Nvidia down 2.9%, Broadcom off 4.6% and Micron losing 4.8%. Major cloud providers also retreated: Alphabet slipped 0.7%, Microsoft dropped 1.3% and Oracle sank 5.8%. At the same time, energy markets were volatile. Oil prices rebounded as Iran stepped up attacks on tankers passing through the Strait of Hormuz and a hurricane threatened US offshore production in the Gulf of Mexico.
